newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Crude Outlook - Steady on Japan utility demand.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook - Steady on Japan utility demand.

text.p: Summer demand is expected to provide support to the Asian crude market this week, as Japanese utilities emerge to cover their requirements for direct burning crudes for power generation.
The lower monthly export volume of heavy grades from Indonesia should also help keep July prices propped up, traders said.
Indonesia's state owned Pertamina allocated 52,000 barrels-per-day (bpd) of Minas crude for July last week, a cut of 10,000 bpd from June.
Duri exports were also reduced by 40 percent month on month to 20,000 bpd.

The cut in volumes was the result of increased demand from Indonesia's 125,000-bpd Exor 1 refinery at Balongan which Pertamina intends to run at maximum capacity to make up for a July maintenance shutdown at its 200,000 bpd Balikpapan refinery.
Balikpapan, which goes down July 10 for about one month, refines mainly light Asian crudes to produce middle distillates.
But the Exor 1 refinery has enough upgrading facilities to produce middle distillates from heavier crudes Minas and Duri.
July trading for the heavy crudes was not fully underway, but initial trades for Minas and Widuri cargoes were at substantially stronger prices compared to June deals, traders said.

But they cautioned that although Japanese requirements in July were likely be the highest this year, the overall demand for oil for power generation was projected to be lower this year than in previous years as utilities increase their dependence on other sources of electicity generation.
This could cap the rise in Minas and Widuri premiums, traders said.
West African and western crudes from Eqypt, North Sea and Argentina, priced against Brent and WTI, continue to flow into Asia, with refiners attracted by the weakness of the western benchmark crudes.
Over 500,000 bpd of western crudes have moved into Asian in the last fortnight.
These arbitrage cargoes were not expected to impact the July Asian crude market as they would not arrive until August.
But the toll on the already bearish Middle East crude market would be greater, as trading for the Middle East crudes moves to August.
The overhang seen in the July Middle East crude market last week was clearing, with the last few cargoes of Oman and Abu Dhabi crudes finally finding homes, albeit at low levels, traders said.
July Oman was last traded at MPM -40, compared to earlier July deals done at MPM -30.
But while discussion on outright August prices of Oman and Abu Dhabi crudes remain notional, competition from the arbitrage western crudes was expected to keep the market deppressed.
The only Middle East crude showing strength was Yemeni Masila.
Masila's official price is set against dated Brent while most other Middle East grades are more closely tied to Dubai crude.
This has given Masila an edge over its competiting crudes, such as Oman.
Several August Masila cargoes were sold at premiums of 14/15 cents per barrel over the third quarter Official Selling Price (OSP) of dated Brent -35.
-- Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3301)
